The **Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS)** is a large-scale, high-completeness [[galaxy-redshift-survey|spectroscopic campaign]] conducted using the [[anglo-australian-telescope|Anglo-Australian Telescope]] to trace [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|galaxy evolution]], [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|mass assembly]], and environmental quenching across the [[redshift-evolution-and-distribution|intermediate-redshift universe]] ($0.3 < z < 1.0$). Designed to bridge the historical gap between comprehensive local benchmarks, such as the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], and high-redshift [[deep-field-campaigns|Deep field campaigns]], DEVILS provides a robust census of the [[cosmic-surveys|cosmos]] over the past 8 billion years [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). The survey targets approximately 60,000 galaxies down to a strict magnitude limit of $Y < 21.2$ mag over $\sim 6$ square degrees, focusing on three extensively studied equatorial and southern regions: the [[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS galaxy catalogue]] field, the [[xmm-lss-survey|XMM-LSS survey]] region, and the [[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|Extended Chandra Deep Field South]]. By utilizing a dynamic "redshift feedback" observing strategy to optimize [[spectroscopic-follow-up|Spectroscopic follow-up]], DEVILS achieves exceptional spectroscopic completeness ($\approx 90\%$), mitigating the structural and environmental selection biases that often plague intermediate-to-high redshift surveys [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract).

A defining feature of the DEVILS framework is its integration of dense spectroscopy with highly consistent, 22-band multiwavelength photometry spanning from the far-ultraviolet to the far-infrared. Utilizing advanced matched-source photometry and self-consistent spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling, researchers have extracted detailed physical properties, revealing that the late-epoch evolution of the galaxy stellar mass function is driven primarily by an increase in the [[cumulative-number-density|Cumulative number density]] of the passive red sequence, rather than shifts in characteristic galaxy mass [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). These precise measurements of [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|Stellar Mass Assembly and Functions]] have also uncovered a distinct bend in the star formation rate-stellar mass relation at low redshifts ($z < 0.45$) and quantified the impact of large-scale structure, demonstrating a $\sim 0.5$ dex suppression in the star formation rates of satellite galaxies as they transition into massive dark matter halos.

Furthermore, DEVILS has profoundly advanced our understanding of the co-evolution of galaxies and their central supermassive black holes. Unified modeling of stellar and active galactic nucleus (AGN) emission has shown that the ratio of the cosmic AGN history to the [[cosmic-evolution-and-star-formation-history|Cosmic Evolution and Star Formation History]] has remained remarkably constant over the past 11 billion years, strongly pointing to a common gas-inflow driver [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract). AGN feedback has also been identified as the primary mechanism responsible for the rapid quenching of high-mass galaxies. Despite these insights, several open questions remain. The exact physical modes of AGN feedback driving this quenching at the dispersion minimum of the star-forming sequence are not fully understood. Additionally, while integrated galaxy light measurements from the survey have helped resolve the extragalactic background light anomaly, demonstrating that known galaxies account for the diffuse optical background, DEVILS data have highlighted a significant $\sim 0.6$ dex discrepancy between dust-derived neutral gas mass densities and direct 21-cm measurements, leaving the exact multiphase distribution of the cosmic baryon inventory a major target for future [[extragalactic-astronomical-surveys|Extragalactic astronomical surveys]].

## Overview and Scientific Motivation

The Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) is a major [[galaxy-redshift-survey|spectroscopic campaign]] conducted on the [[anglo-australian-telescope|Anglo-Australian Telescope]] (AAT). Its primary objective is to map [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|galaxy evolution]] and environmental effects across the [[redshift-evolution-and-distribution|intermediate redshift universe]], specifically targeting the $0.3 < z < 1.0$ regime [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). By observing $\sim 60,000$ galaxies down to a limiting magnitude of $Y < 21.2$ mag over $\sim 6$ deg$^2$, DEVILS spans three extensively studied extragalactic deep fields: the [[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS galaxy catalogue]] field (D10), the [[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|Extended Chandra Deep Field South]] (ECDFS or D03), and the [[xmm-lss-survey|XMM-LSS survey]] region (D02) [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract).

A central scientific motivation for DEVILS is to provide a highly complete census of [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|cosmic mass assembly]] and star formation during a transitional epoch. Historically, large-scale studies of galaxy evolution have been divided into highly complete local surveys, such as the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]] ($z < 0.3$), and deep pencil-beam studies targeting high-redshift galaxies, such as [[zcosmos|zCOSMOS]] [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract), [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). DEVILS explicitly bridges this gap in redshift coverage. Connecting these epochs is essential for tracing the evolution of the stellar mass function (SMF) and the star formation rate-stellar mass (SFR-$M_*$) relation. For instance, combining DEVILS with [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]] data has revealed a distinct bend in the SFR-$M_*$ relation at low redshifts ($z < 0.45$) that is otherwise indistinguishable from a continuous power law at higher redshifts ($z > 2.6$) [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). 

To accurately measure local environmental metrics, such as galaxy group membership and merger rates, surveys require exceptionally high spectroscopic completeness. DEVILS employs a dynamic "redshift feedback" observing strategy—updating target lists in real time based on the previous night's observations—to push completeness to $\sim 90\%$ in fields like COSMOS [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract), [Bravo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250913530B/abstract). Furthermore, representing a departure from earlier color-selected strategies, DEVILS uses a strictly magnitude-limited selection to avoid pre-selection biases against specific galaxy types [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). This unbiased, dense sampling enables robust characterizations of satellite quenching—showing a $\sim 0.5$ dex suppression in star formation for satellites compared to isolated systems—and traces major merger fractions through intermediate redshifts [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541.3220D/abstract), [Fuentealba-Fuentes et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1651F/abstract).

Beyond spectroscopy, the scientific framework of DEVILS relies on consistent multi-wavelength photometric modeling. The survey utilizes the ProFound package to generate matched-source photometry across 22 bands, spanning from the far-ultraviolet to $500\ \mu\text{m}$ [Davies et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.506..256D/abstract). This broad wavelength coverage facilitates the self-consistent modeling of stellar populations and active galactic nuclei (AGN) via advanced spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting codes like PROSPECT [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). Consequently, DEVILS has provided key insights into AGN-galaxy co-evolution, demonstrating that the ratio of the cosmic AGN history (CAGNH) to the [[cosmic-evolution-and-star-formation-history|Cosmic Evolution and Star Formation History]] (CSFH) remains remarkably flat at $\approx 10^{42.5}\ \text{erg}\ \text{s}^{-1}\ M_\odot^{-1}\ \text{yr}$ over the last 11 Gyr, suggesting a common gas-inflow driver for both processes [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract).

## Survey Design and Target Selection

To achieve its scientific goals, DEVILS targets approximately $60,000$ galaxies over a total area of $\sim 6\ \text{deg}^2$ [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). The observations are concentrated in three premier extragalactic deep fields: the [[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS]] field (D10), the [[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|Extended Chandra Deep Field South]] (ECDFS; D03), and the [[xmm-lss-survey|XMM-LSS survey]] region (D02). These fields were specifically chosen for their extensive, pre-existing multi-wavelength coverage.

Target selection for DEVILS represents a structural departure from the color-selection techniques often employed by intermediate-to-high redshift surveys, such as the [[deep2-redshift-survey|DEEP2 Redshift Survey]]. Instead, DEVILS utilizes a purely magnitude-limited Y-band selection based on deep VISTA imaging derived from the VIDEO [Jarvis et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013Msngr.154...26J/abstract) and UltraVISTA surveys. Note that the related VISTA Kilo-degree Infrared Galaxy (VIKING) survey also provides foundational medium-deep near-infrared imaging ($z$, $Y$, $J$, $H$, $K_s$) over $1500\ \text{deg}^2$, which is widely used to sample the rest-frame optical light of galaxies at these intermediate redshifts [Edge et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013Msngr.154...32E/abstract). The primary DEVILS spectroscopic sample is selected to a strict depth of $Y < 21.2$ mag [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). To support this selection and subsequent spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting, the survey relies on the `ProFound` image analysis package. This approach marks a paradigm shift in deep survey design, eschewing traditional fixed-aperture photometry—which has historically been the standard for deriving consistent galaxy colors—in favor of matched-source photometry. This method extracts superior total flux measurements across 22 photometric bands spanning from the far-ultraviolet to $500\ \mu\text{m}$ [Davies et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.506..256D/abstract).

To maximize the efficiency of observing faint targets and optimizing [[spectroscopic-follow-up|Spectroscopic follow-up]], DEVILS implemented a novel "redshift feedback strategy." This approach involves processing spectroscopic data in near real-time and continuously updating the target input lists with the redshift results from the previous night's observations [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). By dynamically removing targets that have successfully yielded a secure [[redshift-catalogs|redshift]], the survey optimizes fiber allocation on the AAT for subsequent pointings, thereby maximizing the integration time spent on the faintest or most spectroscopically elusive sources.

This rigorous targeting and feedback strategy was explicitly designed to achieve exceptional spectroscopic completeness. Reaching this level of completeness is critical for accurately mapping local overdensities, characterizing group environments, and studying satellite quenching without the systematic biases introduced by sparse or incomplete spectroscopic sampling. Final data releases confirm the success of this observational strategy, with DEVILS achieving an impressive $\approx 90\%$ spectroscopic redshift completeness in key regions such as the D10-COSMOS field [Bravo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250913530B/abstract).

## Deep Fields and Multiwavelength Data Curation

The $\approx 6\ \deg^2$ survey area is distributed across three well-studied equatorial and southern fields: D10-COSMOS (overlapping the [[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS galaxy catalogue]]), D02 (the [[xmm-lss-survey|XMM-LSS survey]] region), and D03 ([[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|ECDFS]]) [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). These regions were strategically chosen to build upon the rich legacy of previous [[deep-field-campaigns|Deep field campaigns]], which have accumulated extensive ancillary imaging spanning from the ultraviolet to the radio. The core DEVILS sample comprises approximately 60,000 galaxies selected down to a deep near-infrared magnitude limit of $Y < 21.2$, utilizing imaging from the VISTA-VIDEO and UltraVISTA surveys [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). 

A critical challenge in modern [[extragalactic-astronomy|Extragalactic astronomy]] is the reliable synthesis of multiwavelength photometry. Historically, broad-band spectral energy distribution (SED) catalogs have been compiled using fixed-aperture photometry. While fixed apertures are optimized for deriving robust galaxy colors, they frequently introduce systematic biases when estimating total source fluxes across instruments with vastly different spatial resolutions. To resolve this tension, the DEVILS team implemented a methodological shift toward "matched-source" photometry using the ProFound image analysis package [Davies et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.506..256D/abstract). 

The PROFOUND photometry framework extracts consistent, total-source flux measurements across 22 photometric bands, spanning from the far-ultraviolet (FUV) to the far-infrared ($500\,\mu\mathrm{m}$). This curation integrates state-of-the-art imaging datasets, including high-resolution optical data from Subaru-HSC and VST-VOICE alongside near-infrared data from VISTA [Davies et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.506..256D/abstract). The matched-source PROFOUND approach produces superior total flux estimates that are essential for physically consistent SED modeling, circumventing the artifacts associated with mismatched aperture corrections [Davies et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.506..256D/abstract). Additionally, complementing the broad [[high-redshift-galaxy-evolution|optical and near-infrared datasets]] incorporated within DEVILS, targeted observations from initiatives like the MEGA (MIRI EGS Galaxy and Active Galactic Nucleus) Survey in fields such as the [[extended-groth-strip|Extended Groth strip]] provide vital mid-infrared benchmarks for understanding heavily obscured galaxy evolution at similar epochs [Backhaus et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025AJ....170..300B/abstract).

The integration of this rigorously curated multiwavelength photometric catalog with highly complete spectroscopic redshifts enables precise physical parameter estimation. Using the PROSPECT SED fitting code, researchers have derived self-consistent [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|stellar masses]], star formation rates (SFRs), and metallicity histories for the DEVILS sample [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). Furthermore, the broad wavelength baseline allows for the simultaneous modeling of stellar emission and active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity. The inclusion of an AGN component in these SED fits is crucial; failing to account for AGN emission introduces significant biases in the derived stellar properties and star formation histories of AGN host galaxies [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). Ultimately, by uniting dense spectroscopy with homogeneous 22-band PROFOUND photometry, the DEVILS survey effectively mitigates the biases inherent to both incomplete spectroscopic coverage and heterogeneous imaging, establishing a robust bridge between local universe catalogs and high-redshift deep fields.

## Stellar Population Modeling with ProSpect

To derive robust physical properties from the deep, 22-band multiwavelength photometry assembled by the DEVILS survey, researchers employ the PROSPECT spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting code. Unlike simpler template-matching approaches, PROSPECT utilizes a flexible parametric star formation history and an evolving metallicity history to self-consistently model rest-frame ultraviolet to far-infrared emission [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract).

The derivation of [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|stellar mass]] ($M_\star$) and star formation rate (SFR) is highly sensitive to the assumed priors in SED fitting. PROSPECT modeling demonstrates that the choice of metallicity evolution history can systematically shift inferred stellar masses by up to $0.2$ dex [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). By consistently applying these unified fitting techniques across both DEVILS and the low-redshift [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], researchers resolved a distinct "bend" in the SFR-$M_\star$ relation at $z < 0.45$ that is otherwise indistinguishable from a continuous power law at higher redshifts ($z > 2.6$) [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract).

While gas-phase metallicity is typically measured using auroral or nebular emission lines, its imprint on the overall continuum allows for self-consistent extraction directly via SED fitting. Through this method, DEVILS reveals that the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) undergoes an evolution primarily in normalization, decreasing by approximately $0.1$ dex at $M_\star = 10^{10.5} \mathrm{M}_\odot$ out to $z = 0.3$ [Thorne et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.517.6035T/abstract). By linking present-day gas-phase metallicity to the PROSPECT-derived star formation history, researchers found that at a fixed stellar mass, galaxies with higher metallicities typically formed the bulk of their stellar mass over shorter time-scales and prior to reaching their peak star formation rate [Thorne et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.517.6035T/abstract).

A critical advancement in the DEVILS SED fitting methodology is the simultaneous modeling of an Active Galactic Nucleus (AGN) component alongside the stellar populations. Failing to account for AGN emission is known to introduce significant biases in the derived [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|Stellar Mass Assembly and Functions]] and star formation histories of host galaxies [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). PROSPECT successfully isolates AGN emission in $91\%$ of galaxies pre-selected by traditional broad- or narrow-line indicators [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). 

Integrating this AGN component into the broader galaxy population analysis reveals that at high stellar masses, galaxies frequently exhibit rapidly declining star formation histories strongly associated with AGN feedback. Mapping the specific star formation rate-stellar mass ($sSFR-M_\star$) plane indicates that the minimum in the SFR dispersion, denoted as $M^\ast_{\sigma-\mathrm{min}}$, acts as a physical boundary: below this mass, galaxy evolution is largely governed by stochastic star formation processes, whereas above it, AGN feedback drives rapid quenching and high SFR dispersion [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract). Furthermore, the unified modeling of both AGN bolometric luminosities and stellar histories over the past 11 billion years shows that the ratio of the cosmic AGN history to the [[cosmic-evolution-and-star-formation-history|Cosmic Evolution and Star Formation History]] remains remarkably flat at $\approx 10^{42.5} \mathrm{erg\, s^{-1}\, M_\odot^{-1}\, yr}$. This coeval decline since $z \approx 2$ points to a common physical driver, likely the depletion of the available gas inflow, suppressing both star formation and supermassive black hole accretion identically [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract).

## Evolution of the Stellar Mass Function

The evolution of the galaxy Stellar Mass Function (SMF) provides a fundamental census of [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|Stellar Mass Assembly and Functions]] across cosmic time. To accurately trace this evolution, the DEVILS survey leverages highly complete spectroscopic targeting combined with consistent 22-band multiwavelength photometry, enabling robust mass estimation from the local universe out to $z \approx 9$. 

Stellar masses in DEVILS are derived self-consistently using the PROSPECT spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting code. A key finding from the survey's methodological refinements is that the treatment of galaxy metallicity has a profound impact on mass estimation. Implementing physically motivated, evolving metallicity histories systematically shifts inferred stellar masses by up to $0.2$ dex compared to older models with static metallicity assumptions [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract).

The SMF is typically parametrized using a Schechter function, defined by a low-mass power-law slope $\alpha$, a characteristic turnover mass $M^*$, and a characteristic number density parameter $\phi^*$:
$$ \Phi(M) dM = \phi^* \left( \frac{M}{M^*} \right)^\alpha \exp\left(-\frac{M}{M^*}\right) \frac{dM}{M^*} $$
Historically, there has been ambiguity in the literature—and in standard textbook models—regarding whether galaxy mass assembly over time is predominantly reflected in the steady growth of the characteristic mass $M^*$, or in the [[cumulative-number-density|number density]] $\phi^*$. By applying a homogeneous SED fitting methodology across both DEVILS and the low-redshift [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], researchers mapped the SMF continuously up to $z = 4.25$. The combined data reveal that the characteristic mass $M^*$ and the low-mass slope $\alpha$ remain remarkably static over this epoch. Instead, the evolution of the SMF is predominantly driven by the characteristic mass density parameter $\phi^*$ [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract).

This density-driven evolution is a direct signature of the shifting demographics of galaxy populations, most notably the rapid growth of the red sequence. Observational benchmarks show that over the last $\sim 8$ Gyr (since $z \approx 1$), the characteristic number density and total mass density of the blue, star-forming population have remained largely constant. In stark contrast, the red, passive population has undergone dramatic growth. The number density ($\phi^*$) of characteristic $L^*$ red galaxies has nearly quadrupled, and the total stellar mass density residing in the red sequence has roughly doubled over this timeframe. 

This behavior is consistent with the broader framework of "downsizing" and environmental quenching. As the cosmic star formation rate declines from its peak, massive blue galaxies progressively cease star formation due to active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback and environmental mechanisms, migrating onto the red sequence. This steady flux of quenched galaxies drives the observed increase in the global mass density of passive systems, leaving the characteristic mass of the distribution largely unchanged while significantly inflating the number density of the red sequence. This density-driven evolution is consistent with findings from the VIPERS survey, which mapped a sharp collapse in the number density of massive star-forming galaxies after $z \sim 0.8$, accompanied by a parallel rise in the passive population [Haines et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021essp.confE..51H/abstract).

## The Star-Formation-Metallicity Connection

The Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) utilizes advanced spectral energy distribution (SED) modeling to jointly constrain star formation and chemical enrichment. By employing the PROSPECT SED fitting code, DEVILS incorporates flexible parametric star formation histories alongside evolving gas-phase metallicity models [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). Accounting for metallicity evolution is critical for robust parameter estimation; studies within the DEVILS framework demonstrate that physically motivated metallicity assumptions systematically shift inferred [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|stellar masses]] by up to $0.2$ dex compared to fixed-metallicity models [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract).

This self-consistent modeling enables a detailed mapping of the mass-metallicity relation (MZR) over cosmic time. Analyzing a combined sample of approximately $90,000$ galaxies from DEVILS and the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], researchers find that the MZR evolves primarily in its normalization, exhibiting a shift of roughly $0.1$ dex at a stellar mass of $M_\star = 10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ since $z \sim 0.3$ [Thorne et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.517.6035T/abstract). Crucially, current gas-phase metallicity is intimately linked to a galaxy's past accretion and star formation activity. At a fixed stellar mass, galaxies with elevated metallicities formed the bulk of their stellar mass over shorter timescales and earlier in their lifetimes, prior to their peak star formation rate [Thorne et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.517.6035T/abstract). Furthermore, for massive galaxies ($M_\star > 10^{10.5}\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$) at $z < 0.3$, DEVILS data reveal a distinct anticorrelation between metallicity and current star formation activity [Thorne et al. (2022)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.517.6035T/abstract).

The connection between metallicity and star formation histories provides insight into how galaxy populations transition through the specific star formation rate versus stellar mass (${\rm sSFR}-M_\star$) plane. By combining DEVILS data with low-redshift anchors, astronomers have detected a pronounced bend in the star formation sequence at $z < 0.45$, a feature that is indistinguishable from a continuous power law at higher redshifts ($z > 2.6$) [Thorne et al. (2020)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.505..540T/abstract). The evolution of this sequence—in terms of its slope, normalization, and turnover mass—is driven by the diverse recent star formation histories of the constituent galaxies [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.540.1870D/abstract).

The movement of galaxies across the ${\rm sSFR}-M_\star$ plane is not uniform, but is instead strongly mass-dependent. DEVILS introduces a physical boundary defined by the minimum in the star formation rate dispersion, denoted as $M^*\sigma_{\rm min}$ [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract). Below this critical mass, galaxies exhibit large dispersion in their star formation rates driven primarily by stochastic star formation and a wide variety of absolute sSFR values, even while their overall star formation histories remain relatively flat. Above $M^*\sigma_{\rm min}$, however, high dispersion in the star formation rate is strongly associated with rapidly declining star formation histories. SED modeling indicates that quenching in this high-mass regime is predominantly driven by active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, which disrupts the gas supply and rapidly moves galaxies off the star formation sequence [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract).

## Co-evolution of Active Galactic Nuclei and Star Formation

A major objective of the DEVILS survey is to untangle the interdependent growth of galaxies and their central supermassive black holes. To achieve this, researchers utilize the PROSPECT spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting code, which self-consistently models both stellar and active galactic nucleus (AGN) emission from the far-ultraviolet to the far-infrared [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). Including an AGN component in the SED fits is critical; failing to do so introduces significant biases in the derived [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|stellar masses]] and star formation histories of AGN host galaxies. Through this continuous SED modeling approach, an AGN component is successfully identified in 91% of galaxies pre-selected by traditional broad- and narrow-emission line diagnostics [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract). Using these PROSPECT-derived bolometric luminosities, DEVILS has mapped the evolution of the AGN luminosity function over the redshift range $0 < z < 2$, yielding robust agreement with X-ray selected AGN samples and theoretical predictions [Thorne et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.509.4940T/abstract).

By combining intermediate-redshift DEVILS data with the low-redshift [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], investigators have tracked both the Cosmic AGN History (CAGNH) and the [[cosmic-evolution-and-star-formation-history|Cosmic Evolution and Star Formation History]] (CSFH) over the past 12.5 billion years [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract). Both cosmic histories peak at $z \approx 2$ (a lookback time of approximately 10 Gyr) and exhibit a coeval decline towards the present day. Remarkably, the ratio of bolometric AGN luminosity density to star formation rate density remains strictly flat over the past 11 billion years, taking a constant value of:

$$ \frac{\rm CAGNH}{\rm CSFH} \approx 10^{42.5} \, {\rm erg \, s^{-1} \, M_\odot^{-1} \, yr} $$

This enduring lockstep evolution implies a common underlying physical driver. The simultaneous decline in both processes is interpreted as a direct consequence of the cosmic depletion of the available gas supply, which equivalently throttles both black hole accretion and star formation across the galaxy population [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract).

DEVILS data further elucidate the localized impact of AGN feedback on host galaxies by tracing their trajectories through the specific star formation rate-stellar mass (${\rm sSFR}-M_\star$) plane. Studies of the star-forming sequence demonstrate that the physical mechanisms governing galaxy evolution bifurcate based on stellar mass [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.540.1870D/abstract). While the evolution of low-mass galaxies is dominated by stochastic star formation events, the high-mass regime is fundamentally shaped by AGN feedback. High-mass galaxies that host an AGN are strongly associated with rapidly declining star formation histories [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract). This active quenching becomes the dominant driver of galaxy evolution above a characteristic stellar mass threshold, identified observationally as the minimum in the star formation rate dispersion ($M^\ast \sigma_{\rm min}$) [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract). Consequently, DEVILS confirms that AGN feedback is the primary mechanism responsible for rapidly driving massive galaxies out of the star-forming sequence and into a quiescent state.

## Environment and Satellite Quenching

The Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) is uniquely positioned to map large-scale structure and galaxy group membership at intermediate redshifts ($0.3 < z < 0.5$) owing to its high [[galaxy-redshift-survey|spectroscopic completeness]] ($>85\%$) down to a limiting magnitude of $Y < 21.2$ mag. This dense sampling mitigates the biases typical of incomplete spectroscopic surveys, allowing for the construction of robust galaxy group catalogues and the precise tracking of environmental quenching mechanisms over the past $\sim 5$ Gyr [Bravo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250913530B/abstract).

A primary focus of environmental studies within DEVILS is the phenomenon of satellite quenching—the process by which galaxies transitioning from isolated environments into dark matter halos experience a suppression in their star formation rates (SFR). Direct comparisons between DEVILS and the low-redshift [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]] ($0 < z < 0.2$), using identically derived environmental metrics, reveal that satellite galaxies consistently exhibit suppressed star formation compared to mass-matched isolated systems. On average, satellite SFRs are reduced by $\sim 0.5$ dex in $\log_{10}(\text{SFR}/M_{\odot}\text{yr}^{-1})$ [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541.3220D/abstract). This environmental quenching is strongly dependent on the mass of the host halo; in the most massive dark matter halos, the SFR suppression reaches up to $\sim 1$ dex. Furthermore, satellite quenching is shown to be a time-dependent process, with the fraction of passive (quenched) satellite galaxies having increased by 10-15% over the last 5 Gyr at fixed stellar and halo masses [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541.3220D/abstract).

The influence of the environment on active galactic nucleus (AGN) activity presents a more nuanced picture. While environmental quenching efficiently suppresses star formation, DEVILS group catalogues indicate that satellite galaxies residing in low-mass galaxy groups exhibit no significantly altered AGN properties compared to field galaxies. Conversely, for satellites within [[massive-cluster-survey|massive clusters]], the literature highlights a divergence in AGN behavior: these galaxies show an increased overall AGN fraction, but their average AGN luminosities are decreased [Bravo et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250913530B/abstract). This suggests that while cluster environments may trigger low-luminosity nuclear activity, they simultaneously choke off the larger cold gas supplies required to sustain highly luminous AGN.

## Structural Evolution and Merger Rates

Quantifying the frequency of galaxy mergers is critical for understanding the redistribution of stellar mass and the overall structural evolution of galaxies across cosmic time. In the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS), conducted with the [[anglo-australian-telescope|Anglo-Australian Telescope]], the exceptionally high spectroscopic completeness provides an ideal framework for identifying spatially and kinematically associated galaxy pairs without the severe selection biases that plague highly incomplete spectroscopic campaigns.

Studies of major mergers within the DEVILS fields define associated systems using a projected spatial separation $r_{\mathrm{sep}} < 20 \ h^{-1}$ kpc and a radial velocity separation $v_{\mathrm{sep}} < 500$ km s$^{-1}$ [Fuentealba-Fuentes et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1651F/abstract). For massive galaxies with [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|stellar masses]] of $\log_{10}(M_\star/\mathrm{M}_\odot) = 10.66 \pm 0.25$, the major close-pair fraction is measured to be $\approx 0.021$ at intermediate redshifts ($0.2 < z < 0.34$). 

By combining high-quality spectroscopic, photometric, and grism redshifts to extend the observational baseline out to $z = 0.9$, DEVILS observations constrain the redshift evolution of the merger fraction. When modeled as a power law of the form 
$$\gamma_{m} = A(1 + z)^m$$
the survey yields a normalization $A = 0.024 \pm 0.001$ and a power-law index $m = 0.55 \pm 0.22$ [Fuentealba-Fuentes et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1651F/abstract). This relatively shallow slope indicates a remarkably weak redshift evolution in the merger fraction over the last $\sim 7$ Gyr. These empirically derived close-pair fractions are subsequently converted to physical merger rates using literature prescriptions for merger timescales. The resulting merger rates are highly consistent with predictions from large cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, reinforcing standard models of hierarchical assembly [Fuentealba-Fuentes et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1651F/abstract).

Together, these precise measurements of merger rates and close-pair fractions help resolve the relative contributions of stochastic, merger-driven starbursts versus secular processes in shaping galaxy morphology. While wide-area surveys emphasize that high-mass galaxies formed earlier in a "downsizing" scenario, the DEVILS pair statistics confirm that major mergers continue to play a steady, albeit sub-dominant, role in late-epoch [[stellar-mass-assembly-and-functions|Stellar Mass Assembly and Functions]]. However, literature assessing these structural metrics cautions that cosmic variance remains a significant source of tension in deep, pencil-beam fields. Even over $\sim 0.25$ deg$^2$ footprints, factor-of-two density variations are observed at $z \sim 1$, meaning that the global normalization of intermediate-redshift merger rates remains sensitive to the underlying large-scale environment [Garilli et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008A&A...486..683G/abstract).

## Legacy Science: Lensing and Background Radiation

While the primary goal of the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) is to map the structural and physical evolution of galaxies at intermediate redshifts, its high spectroscopic completeness and robust multi-wavelength photometry have enabled significant secondary scientific gains. In particular, the survey has proven valuable for identifying strong gravitational lenses and constraining the cosmic optical background.

**Searches for Gravitational Lenses**
Deep spectroscopic surveys provide an efficient mechanism for identifying strong gravitational lensing candidates through the detection of blended spectra—individual observations containing the superimposed spectral signatures and redshifts of multiple objects. In the DEVILS Data Release 1, an analysis of 23,197 spectra revealed 181 instances of spectral blending [Holwerda et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.510.2305H/abstract). By leveraging high-resolution imaging from the [[hubble-space-telescope-deep-surveys|Hubble Space Telescope Deep Surveys]] in the D10-[[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS]] field, 57 of these blended targets were visually inspected. This process confirmed 9 classical strong gravitational lensing candidates featuring massive elliptical lenses. 

Although the overall success rate of identifying lenses via blended spectra in the survey is approximately $0.1\%$, the method efficiently identifies highly magnified systems at higher redshifts than previous campaigns such as the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]] and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Such lenses serve as prime targets for high-resolution follow-up, [[extragalactic-supernovae|supernova cosmography]], and searches for magnified neutral hydrogen (H\,{\sc i}) emission [Holwerda et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022MNRAS.510.2305H/abstract).

**Background Radiation and the Cosmic Baryon Inventory**
DEVILS data have also been utilized to measure the integrated galaxy light (IGL), a major component of the cosmic optical background. By combining deep galaxy number counts from DEVILS, the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]], and space-based platforms across multiple photometric bands spanning $0.35$ to $2.2\,\mu\text{m}$, researchers have derived highly accurate limits on the cosmic optical background [Koushan et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503.2033K/abstract). These IGL measurements are consistent with independent gamma-ray constraints on the extragalactic background light to within $\approx 10\%$ [Koushan et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503.2033K/abstract), [Tompkins et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250703412T/abstract). This convergence strongly suggests that the known galaxy population accounts for nearly all of the background light, leaving little room for anomalous or undiscovered diffuse light sources in the intergalactic medium.

In the context of the broader cosmic baryon inventory, DEVILS observations have been used to construct a self-consistent census of baryonic matter confined within galaxies. Models integrating stellar mass, supermassive black holes, dust, and neutral gas indicate that galaxies account for only $\approx 5\%$ of the total cosmic baryon density [D'Silva et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108112D/abstract). The remaining $\approx 95\%$ is presumed to reside as ionized gas dispersed throughout the circumgalactic and intergalactic media. 

However, the literature presents a notable, unresolved tension regarding the neutral gas component of this inventory. Neutral gas mass densities estimated by scaling DEVILS dust mass measurements via metallicity-dependent dust-to-gas ratios are $\sim 0.6$ dex lower than those measured directly by 21-cm radio experiments [D'Silva et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108112D/abstract). This discrepancy remains an open question and may stem from the differing physical scales and spatial distributions inhabited by dust and neutral hydrogen within galaxies, complicating simple scaling relations between the two phases. To better understand these differences, future comparisons will likely draw on insights from dedicated surveys such as JINGLE, a JCMT legacy project that specifically benchmarks the scaling relations between dust and gas in Herschel-selected galaxies [Saintonge et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.481.3497S/abstract).

## Context and Development of Spectroscopic Surveys

The history of [[extragalactic-astronomical-surveys|Extragalactic astronomical surveys]] is characterized by a continuous push to balance survey area, depth, and spectroscopic completeness. Early [[deep-field-campaigns|Deep field campaigns]], such as the Hubble Deep Field, relied heavily on photometric redshifts and morphological classifications. While these efforts successfully detected faint populations, robust measurements of large-scale structure and galaxy kinematics required dedicated [[spectroscopic-follow-up|Spectroscopic follow-up]]. 

During the late 1990s and early 2000s, observational campaigns began mapping the intermediate-redshift universe in earnest. The [[deep2-redshift-survey|DEEP2 Redshift Survey]], for instance, employed strict color-selection criteria to efficiently isolate targets at $0.7 \lesssim z \lesssim 1.4$. While observationally efficient, color pre-selection introduces inherent biases, particularly against red, dusty starbursts or populations with atypical spectral energy distributions. Other initiatives, such as the VIPERS survey, utilized color pre-selection to map large-scale structure and galaxy populations halfway back in the life of the universe [Guzzo et al. (2013)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2013Msngr.151...41G/abstract). In contrast, the VVDS adopted a purely magnitude-limited approach ($I_{\rm AB} \le 22.5$), yielding a much broader redshift distribution that peaked at $z \sim 0.7$ but extended up to $z \sim 5$ [Garilli et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008A&A...486..683G/abstract). 

This magnitude-limited philosophy was further advanced by [[zcosmos|zCOSMOS]], which observed the COSMOS field with the VLT/VIMOS spectrograph. The survey included a magnitude-limited "bright" tier ($I_{\rm AB} < 22.5$) alongside a color-selected "deep" tier ($1.4 < z < 3.0$), specifically designed to map the environments of galaxies spanning scales from $100$ kpc groups to the $100$ Mpc cosmic web [Lilly et al. (2017)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007ApJS..172...70L/abstract). However, even in these pioneering intermediate-to-high redshift surveys, overall spectroscopic completeness rarely exceeded $\sim 70-80\%$, largely due to instrumental constraints such as fiber or slit collisions in densely populated fields.

The critical importance of spatial completeness was demonstrated at low redshift by the [[gama-survey|GAMA survey]]. By employing a highly redundant, multi-visit observation strategy over $\sim 286$ deg$^2$, GAMA achieved an unprecedented target completeness of $>98\%$ down to a limiting magnitude of $r < 19.8$ mag [Liske et al. (2015)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2015MNRAS.452.2087L/abstract). This uniform, dense sampling bypassed the traditional limitations of single-pass fiber surveys, enabling the construction of high-fidelity catalogs for interacting pairs, groups, and clusters. Other pioneering large-scale efforts include the WiggleZ Dark Energy Survey, which utilized the same AAOmega instrument on the [[anglo-australian-telescope|AAT]] as DEVILS to map 400,000 star-forming galaxies, targeting baryon acoustic oscillations at $z > 0.5$ [Glazebrook et al. (2007)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2007ASPC..379...72G/abstract). 

The DEVILS survey was designed to bridge the gap between highly complete local benchmarks like the GAMA survey and distant universe campaigns like VVDS and zCOSMOS [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). While surveys exploring the $z > 1$ universe historically suffered from sparse sampling and strong pre-selection biases, DEVILS extends the GAMA philosophy to intermediate redshifts ($0.3 < z < 1.0$). By targeting purely magnitude-selected samples down to $Y < 21.2$ mag in established deep fields (such as COSMOS and [[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|ECDFS]]) and utilizing a real-time "redshift feedback" strategy to optimize observing efficiency, DEVILS achieves spectroscopic completeness on the order of $90\%$ [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract). This level of nearly complete sampling is essential for robustly defining local overdensities, studying environmental quenching of satellite galaxies, and calculating reliable major merger rates without the structural biases inherent in lower-completeness [[deep-spectroscopic-surveys|Deep spectroscopic surveys]] [Fuentealba-Fuentes et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.539.1651F/abstract), [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541.3220D/abstract).

Contrast this strategy with other concurrent and subsequent surveys, which adopt different methodologies tailored for specific scientific niches. For instance, the [[lega-c-survey|LEGA-C survey]] targeted a smaller, highly characterized sample of $\sim 3200$ massive galaxies at $z \sim 0.8$ in the COSMOS field, utilizing deep 20-hour integrations to resolve detailed stellar population ages and velocity dispersions [van der Wel et al. (2016)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2016ApJS..223...29V/abstract). Similarly, the VANDELS survey provides even deeper spectroscopy—up to 80 hours per source—specifically focusing on higher-redshift ($z > 2.4$) star-forming galaxies and massive passive galaxies in the CDFS and UDS fields [Pentericci et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018A&A...616A.174P/abstract). DEVILS strongly complements these deeper, narrower campaigns by ensuring a highly complete, structurally unbiased sample over a wider intermediate-redshift volume.

## Open Questions and Future Directions

The Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) is poised to serve as a critical spectroscopic baseline for next-generation astronomical facilities. Because the DEVILS target areas (such as the [[cosmos-galaxy-catalogue|COSMOS galaxy catalogue]] field, [[4-ms-chandra-deep-field-south|ECDFS]], and [[xmm-lss-survey|XMM-LSS]]) were specifically selected as deep-drill fields for the upcoming Vera C. Rubin Observatory's LSST [Davies et al. (2018)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2018MNRAS.480..768D/abstract), the survey's highly complete ($\approx 90\%$) spectroscopic coverage at $Y < 21.2$ mag will be instrumental in calibrating photometric redshifts. While studies assessing the detection efficiency of Lyman-break galaxies under varying LSST u-band survey strategies currently rely on simulated galaxy catalogs and analytic models [Crenshaw et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025ApJS..281...54C/abstract), empirical datasets like those from DEVILS will ultimately be essential as real-world baselines. To support this forward-modeling for next-generation facilities like the [[hyper-suprime-cam-surveys|Hyper Suprime-Cam]] (HSC), researchers have developed tools such as the GALSBI-SPS model, which uses DEVILS and GAMA data to generate realistic stellar population synthesis-based galaxy population simulations [Tortorelli et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025A&A...703A.255T/abstract). Furthermore, deep imaging constraints from UltraVISTA photometry are leveraged by procedures like CLIMBER to construct robust mock catalogs, optimizing the scientific output and quantifying mass completeness for upcoming spectrographs such as WAVES and PFS [Pearl et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2022ApJ...925..180P/abstract). Future Stage IV dark energy missions, including the [[euclid-spacecraft|Euclid (spacecraft)]]—which aims to obtain slitless spectroscopy for 35 million galaxies [Linke et al. (2024)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024arXiv240501037L/abstract)—and the Roman Space Telescope, will rely heavily on robust intermediate-redshift calibration samples from campaigns like DEVILS to minimize systematic uncertainties in weak lensing and galaxy clustering measurements. Furthermore, integrating DEVILS data with wider-field campaigns is necessary to overcome the enduring challenge of cosmic variance. Current analyses indicate that even in fields spanning $\sim 0.25$ deg$^2$, density variations of up to a factor of two persist at $z \sim 1$ [Garilli et al. (2008)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2008A&A...486..683G/abstract). Bridging the intermediate-redshift DEVILS sample with broader [[legacy-surveys|Legacy surveys]] will be essential to definitively decouple environment-driven galaxy evolution from large-scale cosmic variance.

A major unresolved frontier in DEVILS research concerns the cosmic baryon inventory and the physical state of the interstellar medium. While DEVILS and integrated galaxy light (IGL) measurements successfully resolve the extragalactic background light anomaly—demonstrating that known galaxies account for the cosmic optical background to within $\sim 10\%$ [Koushan et al. (2021)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2021MNRAS.503.2033K/abstract), [Tompkins et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025arXiv250703412T/abstract)—the inventory of baryons physically confined to galaxies presents a distinct puzzle. The combined mass of stars, dust, neutral gas, and supermassive black holes (SMBHs) accounts for only $\sim 5\%$ of the cosmic baryon density [D'Silva et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108112D/abstract), implying the vast majority of baryons reside in the circumgalactic and intergalactic media. Moreover, a significant tension exists in current neutral gas estimates: the neutral gas mass density inferred from DEVILS dust-to-gas ratios is $\sim 0.6$ dex lower than the density derived from direct 21cm experiments [D'Silva et al. (2026)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2026arXiv260108112D/abstract). Determining the physical processes driving this discrepancy, which likely arises from dust and HI inhabiting fundamentally different spatial scales, remains a key open question.

Finally, the exact mechanisms governing AGN feedback and its role in the global quenching of star formation require further elucidation. DEVILS data reveal that the ratio of the Cosmic AGN History (CAGNH) to the [[cosmic-evolution-and-star-formation-history|Cosmic Evolution and Star Formation History]] (CSFH) has remained remarkably flat at $\approx 10^{42.5}$ erg s$^{-1}$ M$_\odot^{-1}$ yr over the last 11 billion years [D'Silva et al. (2023)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2023MNRAS.524.1448D/abstract). Why these two globally averaged rates track each other so precisely, despite a dramatic decline in absolute activity since $z \sim 2$, is poorly understood, though it strongly points to a common gas-inflow driver. Furthermore, while AGN feedback is strongly implicated in the rapid decline of star formation in high-mass galaxies—specifically at the boundary defined by the star formation rate dispersion minimum ($M^*\sigma_{\rm min}$) [Davies et al. (2025)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2025MNRAS.541..573D/abstract)—the exact physical modes of this feedback remain ambiguous. Future multi-wavelength observations linking DEVILS host-galaxy properties with resolved gas kinematics will be necessary to definitively chart the baryon cycle and the physics of quenching.
